html:
The Coahuiltecans were hundreds of small, independent bands of hunter-gatherers in south Texas and northeast Mexico, along the lower Rio Grande. The name is a modern label; the bands had their own names and probably spoke several languages.

They moved with the seasons, living on prickly pear, mesquite beans, roots, deer and small game. Álvar Núñez Cabeza de Vaca, shipwrecked on the Texas coast in 1528, lived among bands of this region for years and left the first description of them. The Karankawa held the coast to the east.

From the late 1600s Spanish missions drew many bands in, most famously the missions of San Antonio from 1718. Apache and Comanche raids, disease and mission life ended the bands as separate peoples by about 1800. See also Coahuiltecan on the modern map.
